clause.text: 1.01. Distribution Right. The Company hereby appoints and grants Distributor the exclusive right to sell the products of the Company, including the Snotarator™ Nasal Aspirator, ("Products") listed in the current "Price List" (Exhibit "A" attached hereto). The distribution right shall be limited to all countries and all of their territories and possessions within the continent known as South America ("Territory") (Exhibit "B" attached hereto). Distributor agrees that the Products, including the name Snotarator ™ Nasal Aspirator (the "Brand") are the sole property of the Company and Distributor has no interest whatsoever in such Brand and Products, and Distributor shall use the Brand and Products only for so long as the rights granted hereby remains in full force and effect. Distributor shall not take any actions, or aid or assist any other party to take any actions that would infringe upon, harm or contest the proprietary rights of Company in and to the Brand and Products. Distributor shall not assign the rights granted in this Section 1.01 without the prior written consent of the Company.

reviews.rationale: The clause grants Distributor an exclusive distribution right with no stated term, no minimum performance targets, and no lapse mechanism. The no-exclusivity playbook treats an unlimited exclusivity commitment as a high risk if absent, since the preferred policy is non-exclusivity and the fallback caps exclusivity to named products, named territory, and no more than twelve months with minimum performance targets. The grant here names products and a territory but sets no duration cap or performance condition, so it deviates materially from both the preferred and fallback positions. Separately, Section 1.01 only addresses the Distributor's inability to assign the granted rights without consent; it does not restrict the Company's assignment and contains no change-of-control treatment, which is a partial gap relative to the assignment policy but is not the primary driver of the high rating. No IB/indemnity or data-processing obligations are present in this clause, so those positions were not applied.

citations.excerpt: This Agreement is non-exclusive. Each party remains free to provide to, procure from, or contract with any third party for services of the same or a similar kind, without restriction and without any obligation to the other party.

Any exclusivity granted under this Agreement is limited to the named products, the named territory and a period of no more than twelve (12) months, and lapses if the exclusive party fails to meet the minimum performance targets stated in the Order Form.

Neither party may assign this Agreement without the other party's prior written consent, except that either party may assign it in its entirety, on notice and without consent, to a successor in connection with a merger, acquisition or sale of all or substantially all of its assets.

reviews.suggested_fallback: Any exclusivity granted under this Agreement is limited to the named products, the named territory and a period of no more than twelve (12) months, and lapses if the exclusive party fails to meet the minimum performance targets stated in the Order Form.
reviews.verification_reason: The assessment is supported by the clause and cited playbook positions. The clause grants an exclusive distribution right with named products (Snotarator™ Nasal Aspirator/Price List products) and named territory (South America) but no stated duration, no minimum performance targets, and no lapse mechanism, accurately described. The no-exclusivity playbook preferred position is non-exclusivity and the fallback caps exclusivity to named products, named territory, and no more than twelve months with minimum performance targets; the clause deviates from both, supporting the high risk (playbook states high if absent / an unlimited exclusivity is materially off-policy). The assignment observation is also accurate: Section 1.01 restricts only Distributor assignment of granted rights without Company consent and contains no Company assignment limit or change-of-control treatment, a partial gap relative to the assignment policy, and the reviewer correctly treats it as not the primary driver. No unsupported policy or contractual claims appear, and the suggested fallback matches the playbook fallback verbatim.

clause.heading: 1.03. Terms. Terms are net cash upon delivery.

reviews.rationale: The payment timing is not a fixed-day period and falls outside both preferred (Net 30) and fallback (Net 45) benchmarks from receipt of invoice. "Net cash upon delivery" requires payment at or before delivery, which is a more onerous obligation than any playbook position permits and removes the undisputed-invoice and good-faith-dispute withholding protections. It is not high risk because a defined payment obligation exists and the deviation is negotiable, but it materially departs from both preferred and fallback timing, so medium is appropriate.

clause.text:
1.04. Competitive Products. Distributor agrees not to represent or sell other products which are deemed to be competitive with the Company's Products unless agreed to by the Company by written notice.

ARTICLE II MARKETING AND SUPPORT
clause.heading: 1.04. Competitive Products. Distributor agrees not to represent or sell other products which are deemed to be competitive with the Company's Products unless agreed to by the Company by written notice.

reviews.rationale: Clause 1.04 is an unrestricted non-compete/exclusive-dealing restraint: it prohibits Distributor from representing or selling any competitor products indefinitely, with no time limit, territory limitation, performance-conditioned lapse, or defined competing-products scope, and only the Company can waive it by written notice. This conflicts with the playbook's non-exclusivity preference and fails the bounded non-compete fallback, which requires a capped duration (12 months post-termination), a territory tied to actual performance, and a scope limited to directly competing services; the clause instead bars competitive products for the entire relationship with no sunset and no geographic or performance boundary. It also imposes an open-ended exclusive-dealing commitment without the named products/territory, 12-month cap, or minimum-performance lapse permitted under the fallback, and the absence of any customer/partner restriction is separately addressed by the no-customer-non-solicit policy. The salability of competing products is thus materially restricted with no exit other than the Company's discretionary written waiver, which is a material restraint and a missing critical protection under the relevant scope. Two uncertainty notes: (i) the clause is quoted with an unrelated ARTICLE II heading, so the surrounding definitions (e.g., 'Company's Products') and the Term/duration are not supplied, and (ii) because the restraint is expressly for the duration of the appointment with no stated end date, the effective duration could be shorter than 12 months if measured against a fixed schedule, but no dates are given and calendar-month equivalences cannot be asserted, so the duration may also exceed the fallback's 12-month ceiling; that boundary uncertainty does not change the conclusion that the restraint is unbounded and unsupported by the playbook.

One inaccuracy: the rationale states 'the absence of any customer/partner restriction is separately addressed by the no-customer-non-solicit policy'—the clause indeed contains no customer restriction, but the cited source only supplies that policy's preferred position, not an assertion of absence; this is a minor mischaracterization that does not affect the risk conclusion. reviews.rationale: The clause 3.02 force majeure provision is one-sided: it excuses only Company's performance, with no reciprocal relief for Distributor, and contains no prompt-notice requirement, no resumption-as-soon-as-practicable obligation, no express carve-out preserving payment obligations already due, and no termination right after a prolonged event. These omissions deviate from the preferred force-majeure-bounded position (which requires prompt notice, resumption, non-excusal of amounts already due, and a termination right after 30 days) and create material exposure by allowing Company to indefinitely suspend performance. Separately, the clause's exclusion of incidental, special, or consequential damages is only one-directional (protecting Company alone), whereas the retrieved liability-no-consequential-damages position requires mutual exclusion, leaving Distributor exposed to Company's consequential claims. The conjunction of an unbounded force majeure excuse and a one-sided consequential-damages waiver warrants a high risk rating. Note: the clause is labeled 'force majeure' but its text also addresses shipment/FOB delivery and liability limitation; the shipment and passage-of-risk terms are not covered by any retrieved playbook position and therefore are not assessed here. The reference to '3 months' in the prompt is not present in the clause text; no calendar-month versus fixed-day comparison can be made from the supplied evidence.

citations.excerpt: Neither party is liable for a failure to perform caused by an event beyond its reasonable control, provided it notifies the other party promptly and resumes performance as soon as practicable. Force majeure does not excuse an obligation to pay amounts already due, and either party may terminate if the event continues for more than thirty (30) days.

Neither party shall be liable for any indirect, incidental, special, consequential or punitive damages, or for any loss of profits, revenue, goodwill or data, however caused and regardless of the theory of liability, even if advised of the possibility of such damages.

reviews.suggested_fallback: Neither party is liable for a failure to perform caused by an event beyond its reasonable control, provided it notifies the other party promptly and resumes performance as soon as practicable. Force majeure does not excuse an obligation to pay amounts already due, and either party may terminate if the event continues for more than sixty (60) days.
reviews.verification_reason: All claims are supported. The force majeure clause indeed excuses only Company's performance ("Company shall not be in default by reason of any failure in its performance"), contains no prompt-notice requirement, no resumption obligation, no payment carve-out, and no termination right, matching the reviewer's description and deviations from the preferred force-majeure-bounded position. The consequential-damages exclusion ("Nor shall the Company at any time be liable for any incidental, special or consequential damages") is expressly one-directional, while the cited liability-no-consequential-damages preferred position requires mutuality, correctly supporting the deviation claim. The rationale distinguishes what the clause states versus what policy requests, and the high risk rating follows from the conjunction of an unbounded one-sided force majeure excuse and one-sided consequential-damages waiver (relevant policy risk-if-absent levels medium/high). The suggested fallback matches the cited playbook fallback text verbatim. The reviewer correctly notes the absence of any '3 months' reference and makes no unsupported calendar-month/fixed-day comparison. No unsupported claims found.

clause.text: 4.01 Patent Infringement. Company agrees, at its own expense, to indemnify, defend and hold harmless each Distributor and its customers from and against every expense, damage, cost and loss (including attorneys' fees incurred) and to satisfy all judgments and decrees resulting from a claim, suit or proceeding insofar as it is based upon an allegation that any Product or any part thereof furnished by Company or any process which is practiced in the customary use of the Product is or has been infringing upon any patent, copyright or proprietary right, if Company is notified promptly of such claim in writing and given authority, and full and proper information and assistance (at Company's expense) for the defense of same. In case any Product, or any part thereof, if such suit is held to constitute an infringement and the use of said Product or part is enjoined, Company shall, in its sole discretion and at its own expense, either procure for the indemnitee the right to continue using said Product or provide or procure for the Distributor a similar product.

reviews.rationale: The clause grants a broad IP indemnity and defense obligation covering expenses, damages, costs, losses, attorneys' fees, and all judgments and decrees, which substantially tracks the preferred ip-infringement-indemnity position. However, the injunctive-relief remedy is more limited than either playbook position: the preferred position requires payment of damages finally awarded or agreed in settlement, and the fallback offers procure, modify, or refund options. This clause provides only the option to procure the right to continue use or to provide/procure a similar product, omitting modification and refund and expressly reserving sole discretion to the Company. That is a limited deviation from the preferred remedy structure and a residual exposure for the indemnitee, supporting a medium rather than low rating. The prior assessment's reliance on liability-no-consequential-damages was unsupported because the clause contains no consequential-damages exclusion and that policy is not engaged by this indemnity clause.

citations.excerpt: Supplier shall defend and indemnify Customer against any third-party claim alleging that the Services or Deliverables infringe that third party's intellectual property rights, and shall pay any damages finally awarded or agreed in settlement.

reviews.suggested_fallback: Supplier shall defend Customer against any third-party claim alleging that the Services or Deliverables infringe that third party's intellectual property rights, and shall at its option procure the right to continue using the affected item, modify it so it is non-infringing, or refund the fees paid for it.
reviews.verification_reason: The clause text supports the quoted indemnity scope (expenses, damages, costs, losses, attorneys' fees, judgments and decrees). The reviewer correctly states the injunctive-relief remedy differs from both playbook positions: the clause offers only procure-continue-use or provide/procure a similar product, omitting modification and refund, and reserves sole discretion. The preferred position's 'pay damages finally awarded or agreed in settlement' is accurately characterized. The fallback text matches the cited playbook fallback verbatim. The medium risk follows from a broad indemnity largely tracking the preferred position with a limited deviation in remedy structure, consistent with the playbook's medium risk rating. The rationale distinguishes what the clause states from what policy requests, and the rejection of the prior consequential-damages rationale is supported since no such exclusion appears in the clause.

reviews.rationale: The clause imposes a one-way indemnity running only from Distributor to the Company, whereas the retrieved mutual-indemnity position contemplates reciprocal indemnification (each party indemnifies for its own breach/negligence, or at minimum gross negligence/willful misconduct). The clause's indemnity is further narrowed to Distributor's 'fault or negligence,' which functionally maps to the fallback standard, but the absence of any Company-to-Distributor indemnity is a deviation from both the preferred and fallback wording. The IP-infringement-indemnity position is not applicable here because it addresses a supplier indemnifying a customer for third-party claims that the services/deliverables infringe third-party IP; this clause instead concerns Distributor's use of the Company's own mark, a materially different subject, so it does not support a separate risk finding. The clause is bounded to the mark and the Territory and tied to Distributor fault/negligence, tempering exposure. Additionally, no liability-cap carve-out is referenced in the excerpt, so it is unclear whether this indemnity is capped or uncapped; the text does not establish that, and the boundary cannot be resolved from the supplied material. The practical risk is a limited, one-sided indemnity that can be negotiated toward mutuality.

reviews.verification_reason: All contract-characterizing claims are supported: the clause does impose a one-way indemnity from Distributor to Company; it is limited to 'fault or negligence'; it is bounded to the mark and Territory; and the excerpt contains no liability-cap reference, so the capped/uncapped ambiguity is fairly noted as unresolved. The mutual-indemnity policy comparison is accurate (preferred = breach/negligence, fallback = gross negligence/willful misconduct), and the reviewer correctly identifies the absence of Company-to-Distributor indemnity as a deviation from both. The suggested fallback matches the playbook fallback text verbatim, and the risk level (medium) follows from the playbook's 'risk if absent: medium' for a one-sided indemnity. The reviewer properly distinguishes clause text from policy requests and does not assert any unsupported undefined term.

(a) By either party for substantial breach of any material provision of this Agreement by the other, provided due notice has been given to the other of the alleged breach and such other party has not cured the breach within (30) days] thereof; or

(b) By the Company if: there is an unacceptable change in the control or management of the Distributor; if the Distributor makes an assignment for the benefit of creditors; if a petition in bankruptcy is filed by or against the Distributor, resulting in an adjudication of bankruptcy; or, if the Distributor fails to pay its debts as they become due and provided due notice has been given by the Company to the Distributor and the Distributor has not cured such breach within thirty (30) days thereof; or (c) By the written consent of both parties;

8.01 . Confidentiality. Each party agrees to maintain in confidence and not to use except for the purpose of this Agreement any information of a confidential nature such as technical information and data, commercial information and know-how, price structures, administrative and operational costs, or other information relating to each other's business operations or in the case of Distributor to the Brand and Products whether disclosed prior to the Effective Date or thereafter. a) is or became generally available to the public otherwise than by reason of breach by the receiving party of the provisions of this Agreement;

b) was known to the receiving party prior to the date of the Agreement provided that documentary evidence of such knowledge is provided to the disclosing party on request;

c) was subsequently disclosed to the receiving party without obligation of confidentiality by a third party owing no such obligations to the disclosing party in respect of such information;

d) is required by laws to be disclosed but then only when, to the extent reasonably practicable, prompt notice of this requirement has been given to the original disclosing party so that it may seek appropriate relief to prevent or limit such disclosure.

Except as required by applicable laws or court order or as otherwise permitted under this Agreement, all publicity, press releases and public announcements, in each case relating to the Brand and Products in the Territory and/or the transactions contemplated hereby shall be reviewed in advance by, and shall be subject to the written approval (such approval not to be unreasonably withhold) of both the Company and Distributor.
